Small and heterogeneous clinical studies have not established a benefit from broad CSF1/CSF1R-axis targeting in breast cancer, despite encouraging preclinical findings. Accordingly, we highlight a shift toward state-selective, spatially resolved, and temporally coordinated targeting. Emerging approaches include restoring phagocytosis, disrupting chemokine and fibrotic circuits, metabolic reprogramming, and converting suppressive TAMs into inflammatory, antigen-presenting effectors. A major focus is chimeric antigen receptor macrophage (CAR-M) therapy, which combines antigen-directed phagocytosis with tumor infiltration, matrix remodeling, antigen presentation, and recruitment of endogenous immunity. Although early clinical data support manufacturing feasibility, tumor trafficking, and acceptable initial safety, limited antitumor activity underscores challenges involving antigen heterogeneity, persistence, metabolic fitness, biodistribution, and scalable production. We propose a translational roadmap integrating spatial biomarkers, quantitative target selection, macrophage-adapted CAR design, checkpoint-resistant phagocytosis, metabolic engineering, safety switches, and biomarker-guided combination therapy. This framework positions macrophage reprogramming as a context-dependent strategy for modifying selected breast-tumor niches, with therapeutic targets chosen according to the macrophage program and its surrounding cellular architecture. Not applicable. Breast tumors contain spatially organized, multicellular niches in which macrophage functions depend on neighboring immune, stromal, vascular, and malignant cells. Single-cell and spatial profiling reveal diverse macrophage states that cannot be adequately represented by the conventional M1/M2 classification. Macrophage interactions with tumor cells, fibroblasts, extracellular matrix, vasculature, and lymphocytes regulate immune exclusion, invasion, and metastatic dissemination. Therapy-induced myeloid adaptation contributes to resistance to chemotherapy, radiotherapy, endocrine therapy, HER2-targeted treatment, and immune-checkpoint blockade. Broad macrophage-targeting has not established consistent clinical benefit in breast cancer; experimental studies also indicate that depletion can affect macrophage populations with protective functions. State-selective, spatially resolved, and temporally coordinated macrophage reprogramming may provide greater precision than indiscriminate myeloid-cell elimination. CAR-macrophage therapy integrates antigen-specific phagocytosis, tumor infiltration, matrix remodeling, antigen presentation, and activation of endogenous antitumor immunity.

title: Exploring the potential of vamotinib in Ph+ leukemias: is it indeed a 3rd generation tyrosine kinase-inhibitor?
abstract: The development of tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) has markedly improved outcomes in Philadelphia chromosome-positive leukemias; however, resistance mediated by BCR::ABL1 kinase domain (KD) mutations remains a major challenge. While the third-generation TKIs ponatinib and asciminib can suppress many resistant mutations including the gatekeeper mutation T315I, their use may be limited by vascular toxicity and emerging resistance, respectively. Compound mutations (CMs), particularly those involving T315I, are frequent in advanced chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) and Philadelphia chromosome-positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia and are largely refractory to approved TKIs when used as monotherapy. Vamotinib (formerly PF-114), a structural analogue of ponatinib with a narrower kinase inhibition profile avoiding vascular endothelial growth factor receptor-2 (VEGFR-2) inhibition, was developed to retain broad anti-BCR::ABL1 activity while reducing toxicity. Here, we evaluated the in vitro activity of vamotinib against a comprehensive panel of BCR::ABL1 KD mutants using drug concentrations corresponding to clinically relevant dosing regimens and compared the results with available clinical data from a phase-1 trial. Our findings indicate that, even at effective average plasma concentrations corresponding to the maximum tolerated dose, vamotinib exhibits a resistance profile comparable to that of a well-performing second-generation TKI. Notably, high-level resistance persisted for T315I and several P-loop mutations. Clinical responses in mutation-positive patients were largely concordant with these observations. Collectively, these data suggest that vamotinib may not meet the criteria for classification as a third-generation TKI but could have utility in selected patient populations or in rational combination strategies.

title: Plonmarlimab, a GM-CSF-neutralizing antibody, for macrophage activation syndrome
abstract: Macrophage activation syndrome (MAS) is a subtype of secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (sHLH) and a rare, life-threatening complication of uncontrolled rheumatic diseases, characterized by systemic inflammation driven by aberrant activation of macrophages. We aimed to assess the efficacy and safety of plonmarlimab, a high-affinity neutralizing monoclonal antibody targeting granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF), for the treatment of MAS. In this phase 2, multicenter, open-label, single-arm clinical trial (NCT07034209 and CTR20230579), 18 patients with MAS secondary to systemic autoimmune rheumatic disease who were refractory to or had relapsed after high-dose glucocorticoid therapy were enrolled. Patients received plonmarlimab once weekly for 8 weeks at 6 mg/kg as the starting in the accelerated titration stage, and then at 10 mg/kg for the first two doses followed by dose adjustments at the investigator's discretion. The primary endpoint, overall response rate at week 8, was 83.3% (15/18) among all treated patients. The median time to response was 2.1 weeks (95% confidence interval [CI], 1.0-3.1), and the median time to remission of MAS symptoms was 1.1 weeks (95% CI, 1.0-2.3). The least-squares mean percentage reduction in glucocorticoid dose from baseline to week 8 was 79.3% (95% CI, 76.3-82.3), and 83.3% of patients (15/18) achieved a ≥ 50% reduction. No grade ≥ 3 infections were observed. Biomarker analysis showed rapid reductions in ferritin and interleukin (IL)-18 levels. Plonmarlimab showed promising clinical activity and was generally well tolerated in patients with MAS, and IL-18 may serve as a potential pharmacodynamic marker for GM-CSF antibody therapy.

title: Global cancer statistics among older adults in 2024 with projections to 2050: a multi-source population-based analysis
abstract: BACKGROUND: Cancer is the second leading cause of death worldwide and disproportionately affects older adults. As population ageing accelerates, the global cancer burden among older adults continues to increase. This study systematically evaluated the latest global cancer burden and its epidemiological characteristics among older adults. METHODS: Data on the incidence and mortality of 33 malignancies, excluding non-melanoma skin cancer, among adults aged 65 + were extracted from the Global Cancer Observatory (GLOBOCAN) 2024 and Global Burden of Disease Study (GBD) 2023 databases and stratified by age, sex, region, and Human Development Index (HDI). Age-standardized incidence and mortality rates (ASIR and ASMR) were calculated. Annual percentage changes (APC) were used to characterize temporal trends. Decomposition analysis was performed to quantify the contributions of population growth, population aging, and epidemiological changes. Demographic projection methods and generalized additive model (GAM) were applied to forecast the cancer burden through 2050. RESULTS: In 2024, there were 9,966,392 new cancer cases and 6,001,290 cancer deaths among older adults worldwide, accounting for 51.11% and 61.84%, respectively, of all-age totals. Lung, colorectal, stomach, liver, and prostate cancers were leading causes of death. Incidence and mortality were higher in men and increased with age. The Western Pacific Region had the largest burden, whereas Europe Region had the highest ASIR. ASIR correlated positively with HDI (rs = 0.771), while mortality-to-incidence ratio (MIR) correlated negatively (rs = -0.825). From 2000 to 2023, ASIR and ASMR declined, although burden increased, primarily driven by population growth; pancreatic cancer exhibited the most rapid increase. Tobacco use remained the leading risk factor for mortality, while metabolic risks rose in importance. Under a demographic scenario assuming constant 2024 age-specific rates and changes only in population size and age structure, new cancer cases and deaths among older adults are projected to reach approximately 19.8 million and 12.5 million by 2050, roughly double the 2024 figures, with the largest increase in the Eastern Mediterranean region. CONCLUSION: Cancer burden in older adults is substantial, varying by sex, age, region, and development level. Precision prevention and control are urgently needed, particularly in low- and middle-income regions. REGISTRY AND THE REGISTRATION NO. OF THE STUDY/TRIAL: N/A.

title: KRAS in pancreatic cancer: from molecular biology to transformative therapeutics
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a near-universally lethal malignancy, with KRAS mutations driving tumorigenesis in over 90% of cases. For decades considered undruggable, oncogenic KRAS has now been therapeutically engaged across multiple mutational subtypes, a revolution precipitated by allele-specific covalent inhibitors and accelerated by the emergence of RAS(ON) multi-selective inhibitors. The pivotal phase 3 RASolute 302 trial of daraxonrasib, a pan-RAS(ON) inhibitor, demonstrated nearly doubled median overall survival (13.2 versus 6.7 months; HR 0.40; P < 0.0001) over standard chemotherapy in previously treated metastatic PDAC. Concurrently, mutation-selective G12D inhibitors (zoldonrasib, VS-7375, INCB161734), G12D-targeted protein degraders (setidegrasib), G12C-selective RAS(ON) compounds (elironrasib), and next-generation MEK inhibitors (atebimetinib) are advancing through clinical evaluation. This review synthesizes the biological basis of KRAS-driven oncogenesis in the pancreas, the mutational landscape and its prognostic implications, the structural and mechanistic evolution of KRAS inhibitor classes, contemporary and emerging clinical data from recent trials, toxicity profiles and their management, and resistance mechanisms. The field stands at an inflection point: daraxonrasib now redefines second-line PDAC management, while first-line combination regimens with daraxonrasib plus chemotherapy have produced an ORR of 58% in early-phase single-arm data, a result now being tested in the randomized RASolute 303 trial. The challenge ahead lies in translating these results into durable remissions through rational combination therapy and in overcoming acquired resistance.

title: PD-(L)1×VEGF bispecific antibodies in solid tumors: clinical trial updates from ASCO 2026
abstract: PD-(L)1×VEGF bispecific antibodies integrate immune checkpoint blockade and VEGF inhibition within a single molecule, offering a potential strategy to overcome angiogenesis-associated immune resistance. At the 2026 ASCO Annual Meeting, the randomized phase 3 HARMONi-6 trial demonstrated an overall survival benefit with ivonescimab plus chemotherapy over tislelizumab plus chemotherapy in previously untreated advanced squamous non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), extending survival evidence to an active PD-1-based first-line comparator. Exploratory phase 2 studies of pumitamig, SSGJ-707, and HB0025 reported encouraging activity in first-line NSCLC, while phase 1 and 2 studies of IMM2510 and ivonescimab-based regimens suggested activity after prior immunotherapy. Smaller exploratory studies also reported activity in perioperative head and neck cancer, colorectal cancer, endometrial cancer, and mucosal melanoma. Collectively, these findings highlight the clinical potential of PD-(L)1×VEGF bispecific antibodies, with the strongest evidence in first-line squamous NSCLC and broader applications remaining hypothesis-generating. Future development should prioritize predictive biomarkers, resistance mechanisms, optimal treatment sequencing, and careful assessment of immune-related and VEGF-associated toxicities.

title: Futibatinib as a bridge to transplantation and post-transplant maintenance in blast-phase MLN-ZMYM2::FGFR1
abstract: Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with FGFR1 rearrangement (MLN-FGFR1) are rare, aggressive hematologic malignancies for which allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (allo-HCT) remains the only potentially curative option. Pemigatinib, a reversible FGFR1-3 inhibitor, has substantial activity in chronic phase but lower efficacy in blast phase (BP). Data on futibatinib, an irreversible FGFR1-4 inhibitor, in BP MLN-FGFR1 are lacking. We report a 60-year-old man with MLN-ZMYM2::FGFR1 presenting in myeloid BP with extensive extramedullary disease (EMD) that was clinically refractory to induction chemotherapy. Initiation of off-label futibatinib was followed by rapid clinical improvement, complete cytogenetic remission (CCyR) and complete metabolic response (CMR), enabling bridging to allo-HCT from a mismatched unrelated donor. Futibatinib was subsequently continued as post-transplant maintenance with dose escalation and later combined with donor lymphocyte infusions (DLI). At last follow-up (day +497), the patient maintained a CMR and remained in CCyR with full donor chimerism, although ZMYM2::FGFR1 transcripts were still detectable at low levels in the bone marrow by droplet digital PCR. Next-generation sequencing additionally identified a germline DDX41 variant of uncertain significance, a finding potentially relevant to donor selection. To our knowledge, this is the first report of futibatinib used both as a bridge to transplantation and as post-transplant maintenance in BP MLN-FGFR1 with EMD. Although futibatinib's contribution cannot be separated from that of conditioning, graft-versus-leukemia activity and DLI, these hypothesis-generating findings provide support for further evaluation of irreversible FGFR1 inhibition in MLN-FGFR1.

title: A phase Ia first-in-human study of BPB-101, a novel trifunctional antibody targeting the GARP/TGF-β complex and PD-L1, in patients with locally advanced or metastatic solid tumors
abstract: BPB-101 is a first-in-class, humanized trifunctional bispecific IgG1 antibody targeting the GARP/TGF-β complex, active TGF-β, and PD-L1, with preclinical evidence of immunomodulatory and antitumor activity. This phase Ia study aimed to assess the safety, tolerability, pharmacology, and preliminary antitumor activity of BPB-101. A modified accelerated titration design (6, 20, and 60 mg) was followed by a 3 + 3 escalation (200–1800 mg), with intravenous dosing every 3 weeks (Q3W). Eligible patients with advanced or metastatic solid tumors who had received prior standard systemic treatment were enrolled. The primary objectives were dose-limiting toxicity (DLT), maximum tolerated dose (MTD), and recommended phase II dose (RP2D). Secondary and exploratory objectives included pharmacokinetics (PK), pharmacodynamics (PD), immunogenicity, and preliminary antitumor activity. At the data cutoff of January 26, 2025, 19 patients with advanced tumors were enrolled. Treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) occurred in 15 patients (78.9%), with the most common TRAEs being infusion-related reactions (26.3%), anemia (26.3%), and asthenia (21.1%). Grade ≥ 3 TRAEs were reported in two patients (10.5%), both of whom had anemia, with one patient each in the 400 mg and 800 mg groups. No DLTs or treatment-related deaths occurred, and the MTD was not reached. One patient in the 1800 mg cohort permanently discontinued treatment due to an immune-related TRAE (myalgia). BPB-101 exposure increased approximately dose-proportionately at doses ≥ 800 mg. Peripheral PD assessments showed high receptor occupancy (RO) and reductions in circulating TGF-β1 levels in the 1200 mg and 1800 mg cohorts. The 1200 mg and 1800 mg Q3W doses were selected as RP2Ds for further evaluation. Among 17 patients in the efficacy analysis set (EAS), one achieved confirmed immune partial response (iPR) and seven achieved immune stable disease (iSD). The overall immune objective response rate (iORR) was 5.9% (95% CI, 0.1–28.7), and the immune disease control rate (iDCR) was 47.1% (95% CI, 23.0–72.2). BPB-101 showed a manageable safety profile, peripheral PD activity, and preliminary antitumor activity, supporting further evaluation in expansion cohorts. This study was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05869240); part of the study was reported at ESMO ASIA 2025 as an oral presentation. Abstract No: 158O.
